sol.section: §5.2 PT3/PT4 and the definition of 'copies'; §3.4 width dispatch; consistency with §12.6 and §18.1
sol.problem:
PT3 includes 'bitcast' in the rule 'copies (union)', and §5.2 defines copies as 'AV(result) ⊇ AV(operand) lane by lane'. This is false for a bitcast that changes lane geometry. Witness (implicit marker declarations as permitted by §1.5):

target datalayout = "e-p:64:64"
define void @top() {
  %v0 = insertelement <2 x i8> zeroinitializer, i8 1, i32 0
  %v1 = insertelement <2 x i8> %v0, i8 1, i32 1
  %bits = bitcast <2 x i8> %v1 to i16
  %n = zext i16 %bits to i64
  %h = call ptr @__bennett_qalloc(i64 0, i64 %n)
  call void @__bennett_gate(i32 1, ptr %h, i64 256)
  call void @__bennett_gate(i32 1, ptr %h, i64 256)
  call void @__bennett_qfree(ptr %h)
  ret void
}

On the supported little-endian layout, packing the two bytes gives 1 | (1 << 8) = 257. §12.6 emits exactly that packing, then zext preserves 257. The invocation allocates 257 wires, flips wire 256 twice and frees cleanly. LLVM 18 and 23 verify and retain the full witness under default<O0>; instcombine on both folds the allocation operand to 257. Independent native marker harnesses on both majors, for both O0 and instcombine forms, report width=257, gates=2, frees=1, final bit=0 and exit 0. The supplied recogniser instead accepts the O0 witness with AV(bits) and AV(n) containing separate lane-0/lane-1 INT(1) entries and VS(n)={1}. Its normaliser independently emits the correct packed value 257. §3.4 therefore compiles only the width-1 alternative for a materialised width-257 execution. A missing dispatch alternative or allocating one wire and trapping on index 256 violates §18.7. This is a pre-existing PT3 transfer defect, not a regression of the repaired PT10 or PT4 rules.
sol.fix:
In §5.2 remove bitcast from PT3's unconditional lane-copy list and insert this rule:

'PT3 bitcast: A scalar-to-scalar bitcast of equal representation width, or a vector bitcast with equal lane count and equal per-lane representation widths, copies corresponding bit-pattern domains. Every other bitcast uses the DataLayout bit-string packing and resegmentation of §12.6 during S2, before candidate sets, shapes and dispatch domains freeze. Form each source bit string from the represented source-lane bit patterns in DataLayout order, then extract each destination lane or scalar at its destination representation width. For finite integer lane domains, take the Cartesian product of the source domains, pack and extract each result, and apply K to the resulting destination INT sets. Never copy a source-lane INT atom as the value of a packed destination scalar. If a non-handle destination bit-pattern domain cannot be represented by these rules, use non-handle top for that destination; preserve explicit ROOT provenance and apply §6.2's existing restrictions on handle representations. Apply the same rule to constant expressions. This may be implemented by analysing a virtual §12.6 expansion without requiring LLVM optimisation.'

PT4 then applies the actual zext to the packed scalar domain. Add the full witness to DB/DN/DS: verdict=accept; AV(bits)={INT(257)} as one i16 scalar domain, VS(n)={257}; allocated width=257; two successful X gates at index 256; clean free; fault code 0. Verify source, materialised output and instcombine form on LLVM 18/23, and execute a native marker harness that checks the received width and gate index. Add a scalar-to-vector or different-vector-geometry witness to prevent the inverse transfer from remaining a lane-copy rule. A fixed top fallback for all geometry-changing non-handle bitcasts would be sound numerically but would unnecessarily turn this finite width case into BLK-1; use the precise finite packing rule.

codex.problem:
The initial-seeding rule says "Before the fixpoint, seed the initialiser atoms of every global, mutable or constant, into its slots." PT1 gives alloca only "AV ∋ (X, 0)"; no rule seeds its contents. In contrast, §17.1 says "shadow-stack frames and heap allocations are zero-filled in both builds", and §17.3 requires a zero-filled pushed frame. Because §5 mandates the least fixpoint and exact dispatch domains before N24, these rules omit an observable initial value. Witness:

target datalayout = "e-p:64:64-i64:64-n8:16:32:64"
declare ptr @__bennett_qalloc(i64, i64)
declare void @__bennett_qfree(ptr)
define void @top(i1 %set) {
entry:
  %p = alloca i64
  br i1 %set, label %store, label %read
store:
  store i64 1, ptr %p
  br label %read
read:
  %raw = load i64, ptr %p
  %idx = freeze i64 %raw
  %width = extractelement <2 x i64> <i64 1, i64 3>, i64 %idx
  %h = call ptr @__bennett_qalloc(i64 0, i64 %width)
  call void @__bennett_qfree(ptr %h)
  ret void
}

The only explicitly seeded store is INT(1), so PT6 gives AV(%raw)={1}, freeze copies it and the repaired PT10 correctly derives VS(%width)={3}. Both supplied LLVM 18/23 O0 recogniser runs return accept with precisely those sets. On %set=false, N24 instead supplies zero in %p, N8 removes freeze and N15/N21 select lane 0, so qalloc receives width 1; on true it receives 3. I executed the normaliser output with the repository shadow-stack seed and a width-recording marker harness under clang 18 and 23 at O0 and O3: outputs are respectively width 1/live 0 and width 3/live 0, with exit 0. Both original sources verify and retain the witness through default<O0>. This is a contradiction between the mandatory width-3-only dispatch and the specified successful width-1 execution, not a request to define source LLVM uninitialised memory: conformance is to the zero-filled materialised program, and freeze is present in the source. The same missing initialization also affects zero-filled heap objects.
codex.fix: In §5.2 replace the initial-seeding paragraph, before the least-fixpoint sentence, with: "Before the fixpoint, seed the initialiser atoms of every global, mutable or constant, into its slots. For each alloca and allocation-site object, also represent every extent whose initial contents are zero under §§17.1/17.3 as a zero-byte initial image; represent a nonconstant extent symbolically over its possible allocated bytes. Subsequent stores union additional possibilities and never erase these initial possibilities. This is an initial image, not a claim that the object remains immutable." Append to PT6: "For a possibly valid load wholly contained in a zero-filled initial extent, include the all-zero value of the load's representation and width, unioned with values from every overlapping store or copy under the existing interval rules. PT8 propagates these initial byte possibilities when copying memory. Zero contributes no ROOT. Region inputs, replayed caller bytes and other nonzero-initialised contents retain their specified sources; this rule does not replace them with zeros." Add the witness to DB/DN/DS with AV(%raw)=AV(%idx)={INT(0),INT(1)}, VS(%width)={1,3}, verdict=accept, and inputs false/true producing widths 1/3 followed by clean free and code 0. A virtual initialization-store expansion during S2 is an equivalent implementation; I recommend the explicit initial-image rule because it also covers loads at different widths and dynamically sized extents. Do not move the problem to a new rejection, precondition or ISA blocker.

codex.section: §5.2 definition of Copies and PT3/PT4/PT5; §12.6 N21 bitcast packing; §3.4 width dispatch
codex.problem:
Section 5.2 defines "Copies" as "AV(result) ⊇ AV(operand) lane by lane" and PT3 includes bitcast in "copies (union)". This is false for a bitcast changing lane geometry: its result is assembled from bits of multiple lanes, not a lane-wise value copy. Section 12.6 already requires the actual packing and resegmentation, so the S2 transfer contradicts the specified execution. Witness:

target datalayout = "e-p:64:64-i64:64-n8:16:32:64"
declare ptr @__bennett_qalloc(i64, i64)
declare void @__bennett_qfree(ptr)
define void @top() {
  %a = insertelement <2 x i8> zeroinitializer, i8 1, i32 1
  %b = bitcast <2 x i8> %a to i16
  %width = zext i16 %b to i64
  %h = call ptr @__bennett_qalloc(i64 0, i64 %width)
  call void @__bennett_qfree(ptr %h)
  ret void
}

Here %a is <0,1>. Under the specified little-endian packing, %b=0|(1<<8)=256 and %width=256. Copying source lane values can supply only 0 and 1; it cannot supply 256. The supplied recogniser on both LLVM 18/23 O0 outputs returns accept, retains the two source lane maps on the scalar %b/%width, and reports VS(%width)={0,1}. This is not merely an internal representation detail: §3.4 specialises widths from that domain and omits the successful width-256 case. Independent instcombine on both majors folds qalloc's width to literal 256. The N21 output uses zext/shl/or, and native executions of that materialised output with clang 18/23 at O0/O3 all record one width-256 allocation, clean free and exit 0. PT5's generic instruction to evaluate integer casts elementwise does not resolve the explicit conflicting lane-copy rule or specify how source lanes combine.
codex.fix: In §5.2 remove bitcast from the unconditional-copy list in PT3 and add this rule to that row: "A bitcast copies lane by lane only when source and destination have identical lane counts and lane bit widths, treating a scalar as one lane. Otherwise use the virtual N21 bitcast expansion of §12.6: pack the source lane bit patterns into its prescribed bit string, then split that string into destination lanes. Compute the output abstract values through the PT4/PT5 transfers of that expansion; finite INT lane sets denote their full Cartesian product, and the K cap applies to each resulting lane. Unknown bits propagate non-handle top through those transfers. Explicit object and ROOT provenance follows the same expansion and remains subject to §6.2; top never substitutes for ROOT. Apply this rule also to constant expressions and the fixed-vscale form, during S2 before verdicts, candidate sets and dispatch domains freeze." Retain N21's execution semantics. Add the full witness to DB/DN/DS with AV(%b)=AV(%width)={INT(256)}, VS(%width)={256}, verdict=accept, and exactly one width-256 allocation followed by clean free/code 0 on LLVM 18 and 23. Add the inverse scalar-to-vector packing probe as a companion. Direct finite bit-string evaluation is an equivalent implementation of this transfer; I recommend the virtual N21 expansion so analysis and execution share the already decided packing rule. Do not classify this finite, valid case as BLK-1 or reject geometry-changing bitcasts.
